newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Conservation group seeks regulation of caviar trade.
newsitem.headline: Conservation group seeks regulation of caviar trade.

text.p: International trade in caviar would be closely regulated under a German-U.S. proposal to list sturgeons as species requiring protection, conservation officials said Friday.

The secretariat of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), saying overfishing and pollution were threatening sturgeon stocks, recommended its 138 members adopt the measure in Harare, Zimbwabe, next month.

But the Swiss-based group warned it could mean the end of lucrative sales of caviar at airport duty-free shops because hurried passengers are generally not in a position to obtain CITES export permits or certificates from national authorities.
Member states will meet in Harare from June 9-20 to discuss 75 proposals involving 89 species covered by CITES, one of the world's first environmental treaties.

Germany and the United States have proposed including five sturgeon species and 18 "look-alike" species often mistaken for caviar-producing fish on CITES appendix II. The classification covers species not necessarily in danger of extinction but which could become so if trade were not strictly regulated.

Previously, under an agreement with the former Soviet Union, caviar was distributed by Moscow under quotas to the other four countries bordering the Caspian -- Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. Only Russia and Iran are members of CITES.

"It would be in the interest of the five countries for the trade to be controlled. Otherwise, this is a closed sea and the stocks may finish rather quickly just for illegal and Mafia-type structures to make quick money without taking care about what's going to happen in five years," Topkov said.
